# A. Largest Prime Fragment

## How to find it

Factor completely; the sorted final certified leaf is the answer.

## Correctness

Every leaf is prime and their product is the input, so no prime divisor is omitted.

## Complexity

Expected Pollard--rho factorization time.

# B. Carmichael Clock

## How to find it

Compute the exponent of each prime-power unit group, then take their LCM.

## Correctness

CRT decomposes the unit group into prime-power components; an exponent works globally exactly when it is a multiple of every component exponent.

## Complexity

Expected factorization time.

# C. Multiplicative Order

## How to find it

Start from Carmichael lambda and repeatedly divide prime factors while the power remains one.

## Correctness

The true order divides lambda. A division is retained exactly when the smaller candidate is still a multiple of the order.

## Complexity

Two factorizations plus logarithmic exponentiation checks.

# D. Power Congruence

## How to find it

Use the smallest primitive root to convert the power equation to `k*y = log_g(a) mod p-1`.

## Correctness

The primitive-root coordinate is bijective on nonzero residues, and the linear-congruence solver returns precisely its smallest exponent solution.

## Complexity

Factorization plus `O(sqrt(p))` time.

# E. Quadratic Residue Archive

## How to find it

Apply Tonelli--Shanks independently and normalize the two roots by taking the smaller.

## Correctness

Every nonzero quadratic residue has exactly the pair `x,p-x`; zero has one root.

## Complexity

`O(q log squared p)` operations.

# F. Affine Exponent Meeting

## How to find it

Take a discrete log inside the subgroup generated by `a`, find its order, then solve the affine exponent congruence modulo that order.

## Correctness

Powers of `a` agree exactly when exponents agree modulo its order, so the final linear congruence is necessary and sufficient.

## Complexity

Factorization plus BSGS per query.
